pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4): complete metamorphosis in detail — egg → larva → pupa → adult, with correct terms. The larva (caterpillar, grub, maggot) looks TOTALLY different from the adult; inside the pupa the body is rebuilt. Butterflies, beetles, flies and ladybirds all do this.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4/Y5 life-cycle content ('describe the differences in the life cycles of different animals'; life cycle of an insect). Builds on the KS1 butterfly observation.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS1-1 (organisms have diverse life cycles; all include birth, growth, reproduction, death).
• Operational details — the new depth beyond KS1 is (a) the correct generalised terms (larva/pupa, not just caterpillar/chrysalis), (b) that MANY insects share this pattern (not just butterflies), and (c) WHAT each stage is for — larva eats/grows, pupa rebuilds. The rebuild-inside-the-pupa is the astonishing, load-bearing idea. Contrast larva→adult radical difference with animals whose young resemble adults (sets up incomplete metamorphosis later).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): names the four stages with correct terms. Tier B (age 8): says what the larva stage and pupa stage are FOR (eat/grow; transform). Tier C (age 9): gives two insects that undergo complete metamorphosis and explains that the larva looks nothing like the adult because the body is rebuilt in the pupa.
bestPractices: Introduce the generalised terms (larva, pupa) alongside the familiar ones and use them across several insects, not just butterflies.
Teach the FUNCTION of each stage — larva eats and grows, pupa rebuilds — not just the names.
Make the pupa reorganisation explicit and vivid; it is the astonishing, memorable core.
Generalise across species (butterfly, beetle, fly, ladybird) so children see a shared pattern, not a butterfly-only story.
Exploit the radical larva-adult difference (maggot→fly) to motivate 'why so different?' and set up incomplete metamorphosis later.
keyRepresentations: A four-stage cycle diagram with correct terms (egg, larva, pupa, adult).
A pupa cutaway showing the body reorganising.
A multi-species comparison (same four stages for butterfly/beetle/fly).
commonMisconceptions: 'Only butterflies do metamorphosis' — beetles, flies, bees and many others share the pattern.
'The larva and adult are different animals' — they are the same individual, transformed.
'The pupa is asleep/resting' — it is actively being rebuilt inside.
'The larva just gets bigger and grows wings' — the body is reorganised, not merely enlarged.
'Caterpillar/chrysalis are the only correct words' — larva/pupa are the general terms across insects.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9, teach complete metamorphosis in detail: egg → larva → pupa → adult, using the correct generalised terms (larva/pupa) alongside the familiar ones (caterpillar/chrysalis). The load-bearing ideas are (a) the function of each stage — the larva eats and grows, the pupa is where the body is reorganised into the adult — and (b) that many insects share this pattern, not just butterflies. Exploit how radically different the larva looks from the adult (maggot→fly, grub→beetle) to motivate 'why so different?' and prepare for incomplete metamorphosis later.

activities.title: Build and run the four-stage cycle, then reveal the rebuild
feedback: If a learner orders the stages wrongly or swaps terms, anchor to a known example (egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly) and match each formal term to the familiar stage before generalising.
If a learner says the pupa is 'resting' or 'sleeping', contrast before/after of the inside: the body is being actively reorganised, not resting or eating.
If a learner assigns eating/growing to the pupa, split the jobs by stage: larva = eat/grow; pupa = transform.
Confirm the generalisation: 'You ran the same four stages for a beetle and a fly — so what does that tell you about how many insects develop this way?'
activities.rationale: Coupling an ordered cycle with the function of each stage, and running the same cycle across species, makes 'rebuilt inside the pupa' and 'many insects do this' concrete rather than a memorised list. A sequencing step, cutaway reveal, and species switcher are optional interactions that may make the mechanism visible; their efficacy is not independently validated here.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils describe the differences in the life cycles of a variety of animals, including the life cycle of an insect.
Complete metamorphosis (holometaboly: egg→larva→pupa→adult) occurs in butterflies, beetles, flies, bees and others; the larva differs radically from the adult and the body is reorganised in the pupa.
learnerActions: Arrange the four stages of a butterfly's life cycle in the correct order using the proper terms: egg → larva → pupa → adult.
Examine the larva stage and state its one main job: eating and growing (shedding its skin as it swells).

Reveal what is happening inside the pupa — much of the larva's body is broken down, and groups of cells that were already in the larva build adult parts such as wings, legs and new eyes — and describe in your own words that the insect is actively rebuilt, not just enlarged or sleeping.
Run the SAME four stages for a beetle (egg → grub → pupa → beetle) and a housefly (egg → maggot → pupa → fly), and state that this is a shared insect pattern rather than a butterfly-only story.
activities.intendedInsight: Complete metamorphosis is an ordered, four-stage process shared by many insects, in which the larva's job is to eat and grow and the pupa is where the body is actively reorganised into the adult.

activities.title: Match the young to the grown-up
feedback: If a learner treats the larva and adult as two different animals, track one named individual through all four stages as the same insect.
If surprised that a maggot becomes a fly, connect to the familiar caterpillar-to-butterfly case to show the shared pattern.
Reinforce: 'They look completely different because the body was reorganised inside the pupa.'
activities.rationale: A matching task can exploit the radical larva-adult difference to confront the misconception that they are separate animals and to reinforce the role of the pupa. Note that matching checks recognition; include a 'why' prompt so the learner also produces the explanation.
sourceClaims: Complete metamorphosis (holometaboly: egg→larva→pupa→adult) occurs in butterflies, beetles, flies, bees and others; the larva differs radically from the adult and the body is reorganised in the pupa.
learnerActions: Match each larva to the adult it becomes: maggot→fly, grub→beetle, caterpillar→butterfly.
For each pair, explain why the larva and adult look so different: the body was reorganised inside the pupa.
State that the larva and adult are the SAME individual at different stages, not two different animals.
activities.intendedInsight: The larva looks nothing like the adult because the body is rebuilt in the pupa — but it is the same insect transformed, not a separate creature.

activities.title: Which stage does which job?
feedback: A fully correct response orders the four stages, assigns larva = eat/grow and pupa = transform, gives two examples, and recognises the grasshopper as NOT complete metamorphosis.
If a learner names and orders the stages but can't assign functions, that is partial understanding — probe: 'Why does the caterpillar eat so much before the pupa?'
If a learner calls the grasshopper complete metamorphosis, point out it has no pupa and its young already resemble the adult.
activities.rationale: Adding a function question — which stage does which job — plus a no-pupa counterexample discriminates a memorised sequence from genuine understanding of the process; the counterexample also draws on comparing differences between animals' life cycles.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils describe the differences in the life cycles of a variety of animals, including the life cycle of an insect.
learnerActions: State the four stages in the right order: egg → larva → pupa → adult.
Say in which stage the insect does most of its eating and growing (larva) and in which stage its body is being rebuilt (pupa), and explain how you know.
Give at least two insects that undergo complete metamorphosis (e.g. butterfly and beetle).

Consider a counterexample: a grasshopper hatches as a young grasshopper (a nymph) that looks like a small adult without working wings, and it grows by shedding its skin several times, with wings developing gradually and no pupa — decide whether that is complete metamorphosis and justify your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding is shown by assigning the correct function to each stage and by recognising that an insect with no pupa (young resembling the adult) is NOT complete metamorphosis — not merely by reciting the order.

activities.title: In-role larva interview (optional engagement)
feedback: Prompt for accuracy: 'What happens to your body inside the pupa — do you just get bigger, or is something else going on?'
Steer away from 'sleeping': the body is being reorganised.
activities.rationale: A light in-role format may motivate recall and prediction, though ordering and comparing tasks teach the shared pattern more directly; use this as a warm-up or extension rather than the core. Its effectiveness relative to other formats is not validated here.
learnerActions: Take on the role of a larva (caterpillar, grub or maggot) and answer 'What will you turn into, and how?'
Describe the stages still to come (pupa, then adult) and what happens inside the pupa.
activities.intendedInsight: Narrating the transformation from the larva's point of view can rehearse the stage order and the rebuild idea in an engaging way.

constraints: Introduce the generalised terms (larva, pupa) alongside the familiar ones (caterpillar, chrysalis) and use them across several insects, not just butterflies.
Teach the FUNCTION of each stage — larva eats and grows, pupa reorganises the body — not only the names.
Make the pupa reorganisation explicit and vivid: it is the astonishing, memorable core, and the insect is NOT resting or eating there.
Generalise across species (butterfly, beetle, fly, ladybird) so children see a shared pattern.

A fixed labelled diagram with a tap-to-reveal pupa cutaway can teach the terms and the rebuild clearly; it simply cannot be re-run across species by the learner, so pair it with a multi-species comparison if the generalisation is the goal.

A 3D pupa-interior cutaway is an optional alternative only where such an asset exists; the ordered-process-with-reveal concept is well served in 2D, so 3D is not required and should not be presented as adding nothing.

Recognition/matching and ordering tasks check sequence and function but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own explanation of the rebuild — include at least one prompt for independent explanation.
The grasshopper counterexample sets up incomplete metamorphosis; do not present it as complete metamorphosis.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
All three source claims are marked verified:false in the original row; treat standards citations and the entomology reference as unconfirmed.

Original framing called a coded 2D interactive 'ideal' and implied a static image 'can't' drive the generalisation; this has been softened to a stated affordance/limit (a fixed diagram can still teach the terms and rebuild) rather than a universal claim about what can or cannot teach.

The NGSS 3-LS1-1 claim is not cited in any activity's sourceClaims: it is topical to life cycles generally but does not directly support the specific teaching principles (function assignment / discriminating understanding).
Internal assessment-method vocabulary ('two-tier'/'second tier') was removed from the learner-facing title and rationale while preserving the underlying two-level diagnostic design.

Self-audit: stage order egg→larva→pupa→adult, the larva=eat/grow and pupa=transform functions, and the maggot→fly / grub→beetle / caterpillar→butterfly pairings are internally consistent with the diagnostic and misconception fields; no arithmetic or logic errors found. The grasshopper is correctly characterised as not complete metamorphosis (no pupa, young resemble adult). The 'body dissolving and re-forming' wording is a child-appropriate simplification consistent with the original.

probeDeeper: 'You said larva is the eating stage. So why does the caterpillar eat so much before it becomes a pupa?'
'What is actually happening inside the pupa — is the insect resting, or is something else going on?'
'A grasshopper hatches as a tiny grasshopper and just gets bigger — no pupa at all. Does it go through complete metamorphosis?' (incomplete-metamorphosis counterexample)
'A maggot turns into a fly. Which four stages did it go through — and is that the same set as the butterfly's?'
assess.correctAnswer: The four stages in order are: egg → larva → pupa → adult. The insect does most of its eating and growing in the LARVA stage (the caterpillar, grub or maggot — which looks completely different from the adult). The body is rebuilt in the PUPA stage (the chrysalis/cocoon), where the larva's body is reorganised into the adult. Butterflies, beetles, flies and ladybirds all go through these four stages.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the larva (caterpillar/grub/maggot) is a different animal from the adult, not an earlier stage of the same insect
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track one named individual through all four stages as the SAME insect. Emphasise the larva looks different but IS the young form — build on the caterpillar-to-butterfly idea.
errorPatterns.distractor: The larva and the adult are two different animals
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats larva and adult as separate creatures; surprised a maggot becomes a fly

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the insect keeps eating and growing in the pupa, or that the pupa is just resting/sleeping with no change
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split the two jobs by stage: larva = the eating/growing stage; pupa = the transforming stage where the body is reorganised (not sleeping, not eating). Use before/after images of what's inside.
errorPatterns.distractor: The insect keeps eating and growing inside the pupa
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: assigns eating/growing to the pupa, or calls the pupa 'sleeping'; can't say the body is rebuilt there

errorPatterns.pattern: Muddles the stage order or terms — e.g. puts pupa before larva, or uses 'cocoon/egg' interchangeably
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the order with a known example (egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly) then generalise the formal terms onto it, matching each term to the familiar stage.
errorPatterns.distractor: The order is egg → pupa → larva → adult
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders the stages wrongly or swaps the terms; can't reliably say egg→larva→pupa→adult

responseLevels.gap: Can't order the four stages, or treats the larva as a separate animal; no sense of which stage does what.
responseLevels.full: Orders the four stages AND assigns the functions (larva eats/grows; pupa is where the body is rebuilt), gives two examples, AND transfers — e.g. recognises a grasshopper with no pupa is NOT complete metamorphosis, showing understanding beyond a memorised list.
responseLevels.partial: Names and orders egg→larva→pupa→adult but can't assign functions — doesn't reliably say larva = eat/grow and pupa = transform, or thinks the pupa is 'sleeping'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A butterfly and a beetle both go through complete metamorphosis. Name the four stages in the right order, and tell me: in WHICH stage does the insect do most of its eating and growing, and in which stage is its body being rebuilt? Explain how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the concept orders four stages AND assigns the FUNCTIONS correctly — larva = eat/grow, pupa = transform. A child with only a memorised sequence gets the order but can't say which stage does what, or thinks the pupa is where it eats, or that the larva is a different animal. The second tier (which stage does which job) is what separates a labelled sequence from an understood one.
